boards.test: Speed: output tokens per second on a short chat (median of 3 after a warm-up). Memory: peak during a 4,096-token prompt. Quality: how often the version picks the same next word as a near-lossless 8-bit copy (top-1 match), plus 10 short questions with one right answer.
boards.source_note: Entered from the factory report as posted on the day; the full result files are on the Mac mini. Rows marked 'about' will be exact after the next run.
boards.takeaway: the standard 4-bit build is still the best tradeoff. Speed tracks how many bits each weight uses, and below 4 bits quality drops sharply. Next to try: DWQ 3-bit.

boards.test: 500 GSM8K grade-school math problems (openai/gsm8k test, seed 0), the same for every version, served the way Smarty Pants serves Smarty: thinking off, greedy, up to 1,024 tokens. DWQ builds: mlx-lm DWQ, 1,024 samples, group size 64. A version is better only with more right answers at McNemar p < 0.05; faster counts only if the 95% interval of the accuracy change stays above -2 points. Script: scripts/model-factory/benchcheck.py.
boards.takeaway: neither DWQ build beats the one we serve. 3-bit DWQ is about 20% faster and 13% smaller but gets about 5 points fewer right; 4-bit DWQ is no different. The served build stays. We keep negative results on the page.

rows.label: DWQ 3-bit (tuned to copy the full model)
rows.why: faster and smaller, but 2.5 to 8.3 points fewer right

rows.label: DWQ 4-bit (tuned to copy the full model)
rows.why: same speed, no real difference in right answers

boards.test: draft-ahead (speculative) decoding: a small guesser model, mlx-community/Qwen3.5-0.8B-MLX-4bit, proposes 2 or 4 words and Smarty checks them in one pass. Same 500 GSM8K problems and served settings as above (thinking off, greedy, up to 1,024 tokens); the standard build was timed again in the same sitting. Guesses accepted: 85% (2 at a time), 76% (4 at a time).
boards.takeaway: no win yet. Guessing 4 ahead is 10% faster with the same right answers, but it needs 18% more memory, and our rule allows at most 5% more. Guessing 2 ahead is slower.

rows.label: Standard 4-bit + guess 4 words ahead
rows.why: 10% faster, same right answers, but 18% more memory

boards.test: Speed: output tokens per second on a short chat (median of 3 after a warm-up). Memory: peak during a 4,096-token prompt. Quality: how often the version picks the same next word as a near-lossless 8-bit copy (top-1 match), plus 10 short questions with one right answer. mlx 0.32.4.
boards.source_note: Entered from the factory report as posted on the day; the full result files are on the Mac mini. Rows marked 'about' will be exact after the next run.
boards.takeaway: the standard 4-bit build runs well on a 32 GB+ Mac; neither tested change helped.

boards.test: draft-ahead (speculative) decoding: the small mlx-community/Qwen3.5-0.8B-MLX-4bit guesses 4 words at a time and Qwen 3.8 27B checks them in one pass; 76% of guesses were kept. 200 GSM8K problems, the same for both, measured with mlx-lm in Python, greedy, thinking off, up to 1,024 tokens. The standard build was timed again in the same sitting, with serving paused (this sitting's standard speed is lower than the 35.7 tok/s chat test above, which used a different prompt and length).
boards.takeaway: draft-ahead made Qwen 3.8 27B 81% faster with the same right answers and only 3% more memory, the first speed-up to beat a standard build on this page.
boards.caution: Important: this gain was measured greedy with thinking off. When our Mac app served it live at its default settings (temperature 0.6, thinking on), we did not see the speed-up, so the app has draft-ahead turned off again while we find out why. Do not expect this speed from Smarty Pants today.

rows.label: Standard 4-bit + guess 4 words ahead (test only, off in the app)
rows.why: 81% faster, same right answers, 3% more memory (in this test setup; not yet in the live app)

boards.test: the full GSM8K test (1,319 problems), the same for both, served the way Smarty Pants serves it: thinking off, greedy, up to 1,024 tokens. Better needs answers as good (95% interval of the accuracy change above -2 points) plus at least 10% faster or 10% less memory. In the Mac app's own code, at temperature 0.6 with thinking on, the smaller build also ran faster: 20.3 vs 17.6 tok/s.
boards.takeaway: the smaller tuned build gives the same answers (94.6% vs 94.8%, no real difference) while running 15% faster on 15% less memory, so it fits more Macs.
boards.credit: the 3.80-bits-per-weight DWQ build is by AtomicChat ([AtomicChat/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-AD-3.80bpw-DWQ-13.7GB](https://huggingface.co/AtomicChat/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-AD-3.80bpw-DWQ-13.7GB), revision 9fa7ab0); we tested it.

boards.test: Speed: output tokens per second on a short chat (median of 3 after a warm-up). Memory: peak during a 4,096-token prompt. Quality: how often the version picks the same next word as a near-lossless 8-bit copy (top-1 match), plus 10 short questions with one right answer. The yardstick is a community 8-bit copy (pjain001/arete-27b-8bit-mlx); bf16 did not fit the Mac's free disk. Also checked on 300 GSM8K math problems (thinking off, greedy, up to 1,024 tokens): the 4-bit build got 94.3% right.
boards.takeaway: the 4-bit build passes: 10/10 checks, 94.3% on GSM8K (in line with Qwen 3.8 27B, which it is fine-tuned from), 35.5 tok/s and an 18.3 GB peak. That fits 32 GB+ Macs comfortably and 24 GB Macs only tightly.
boards.credit: Arete 27B is by NousResearch (Apache-2.0); the 4-bit MLX build is by Duckets ([Duckets/Arete-27B-MLX-4bit](https://huggingface.co/Duckets/Arete-27B-MLX-4bit), revision bd3f716).

boards.test: Speed: output tokens per second on a short chat (median of 3 after a warm-up). Memory: peak during a 4,096-token prompt. Quality: how often the version picks the same next word as a 6-bit copy (the quality yardstick here) (top-1 match), plus 10 short questions with one right answer. mlx 0.32.4, mlx-lm 0.32.2.
boards.takeaway: the standard 4-bit build passes all 10 checks at about 158 tok/s and 21.5 GB, so it fits Macs with 48 GB or more. Mixed 3/4-bit saves memory but loses too much quality.
boards.caution: Our own 4-bit build timed 34% faster than the community build, but that is unconfirmed: it has the same bits and memory, and the community build was timed right after a long download. We will rerun it before relying on it.

rows.label: 4-bit, our own build
rows.why: timed 34% faster with the same quality; needs a repeat run

rows.label: Mixed 3/4-bit
rows.why: 17% less memory, but 25% slower and perplexity +13.5%

boards.test: 300 GSM8K math problems, thinking off, greedy, up to 2,048 tokens. Single build tested (no yardstick copy).
boards.takeaway: passes: 92.3% right at 74.7 tok/s and a 21.1 GB peak, so it fits Macs with 32 GB or more. For comparison on the same test: Qwen 3.8 27B 94.6% (all 1,319 problems), Arete 27B 94.3% at 35.5 tok/s.
boards.credit: Axion 1.0 35B is by Axion1-0 (Apache-2.0); the UD 4-bit MLX build is by NapYang ([NapYang/Axion-1.0-35B-UD-MLX-4bit-fp16](https://huggingface.co/NapYang/Axion-1.0-35B-UD-MLX-4bit-fp16), revision be0c767).

boards.test: Speed: output tokens per second on a short chat (median of 3 after a warm-up). Memory: peak during a 4,096-token prompt. Quality: how often the version picks the same next word as our yardstick copy (top-1 match), plus 10 short questions with one right answer. mlx 0.32.4, mlx-lm 0.32.2.
boards.caution: The yardstick is not a true 8-bit copy: the converter kept OpenAI's own 4-bit expert weights, so it came out at 4.6 bits per weight. Quality here means closeness to a near-original copy, not to a higher-precision one.
boards.takeaway: both community 4-bit builds run at about 100 tok/s and peak at 12-13 GB, so they fit 24 GB Macs. OptiQ is a trade-off rather than a win: much closer to the original (top-1 85.8% vs 66.6%, 9/10 checks vs 7/10) for 6% less speed. A math accuracy test comes next.

rows.label: OptiQ 4-bit (mlx-community)
rows.why: much closer to the original and 2 more checks right, 6% slower, 0.45 GB more

boards.test: speed only: one request at a time, 500 to 4,096-token prompts, 128 tokens out, mlx-vlm 0.7.0. With 8 requests at once the Mac produced 193 tok/s in total. No quality test yet.

reranking 150 queries (3,000 query-document pairs) from mteb/askubuntudupquestions-reranking; score = probability of "yes" after Qwen's reranker prompt. Speed is pairs per second at batch size 8 over a short window, so treat it as rough (batch 1: bf16 68.8, mxfp8 51.9, ours 48.4; batch 32: 138.2, 95.1, 93.6).
boards.takeaway: a trade-off, not a win. On a 0.6B model the 8-bit builds save only about 0.6 GB and are not faster overall; ranking quality differences are within noise. The bf16 build is the one we serve. Our 8-bit build agrees with bf16 on the top pick far more often than the mxfp8 build (96% vs 85%).

rows.label: mxfp8 (mlx-community)
rows.why: 0.6 GB less memory; faster at batch 8 but slower at batch 1 and 32

rows.label: 8-bit, our own build (group 64, not released)
rows.why: 0.6 GB less memory, closest to bf16, but slower

boards.test: 30 MATH-500 math problems (seeded random pick), thinking on, up to 32,768 tokens, MIT's sampling settings, 1 answer per problem, graded with math-verify 0.9.0 by MIT's rule. Runs on MLX in bfloat16 rather than vLLM, so single answers are not comparable one to one with MIT's.

rows.label: Qwen3.5-0.8B + MIT CSAIL's p50c weight edit (reproduced)
rows.why: finished 60% of answers (was 7%), ended in a loop 3% (was 87%)

boards.takeaway: the edit changes 0.016% of the weights. On our Mac it cut loops from 87% to 3% and raised correct answers from 7% to 33%, with no change in speed or memory. Problem by problem, the edited model got 8 right that the original missed and lost none (sign test p ≈ 0.008). MIT reports 7.9% to 48.1% on all 500 problems with 4 answers each.
boards.credit: this is a reproduction of MIT CSAIL's published edit (Takehi, Teoh, Zhang and Khattab, [weight-space programming](https://rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming), edit and evaluation code from [RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs](https://github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs)). Smarty Pants did not make this edit; we rebuilt it bit for bit, hash-checked it and measured it on a Mac.
